objectiveEnglish: Explain a wrong coffee and missing pastry politely in French.
focusFrench: Signaler une erreur avec je crois que ; opposer deux boissons avec pas ; dire qu'il me manque un article.
focusEnglish: Use je crois que to soften a correction, pas to contrast items, and il me manque for a missing item.

cards.note: In many cafés in France, a similar drink is ordered as un café allongé.
In cafés in France, this is often ordered as un crème or un café crème.

Pan dulce is the common name for sweet pastries in Mexican and US Spanish. It is kept here as a named item, as it would appear on the menu. French has no single exact equivalent; in a French bakery you would name the specific item, for example un croissant or une brioche.
For a woman, say la serveuse.

cards.targetFrench: Excusez-moi, je crois qu'il y a une erreur dans ma commande.
cards.supportEnglish: Excuse me, I think there is a mistake with my order.
cards.sourceSpanish: Disculpe, creo que hay un error con mi pedido.
cards.note: Use vous with one staff member.

cards.targetFrench: J'ai commandé un americano, pas un café au lait.
cards.supportEnglish: I ordered an americano, not a coffee with milk.
cards.sourceSpanish: Pedí un café americano, no un café con leche.

cards.targetFrench: Il me manque un pan dulce.
Pouvez-vous me l'échanger, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.supportEnglish: Can you change it for me, please?

cards.targetFrench: Pouvez-vous vérifier ma commande, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.supportEnglish: Can you check my order, please?

reader.targetFrench: J'arrive au comptoir et je commande un americano et un pan dulce.
reader.supportEnglish: I get to the counter and order an americano and a pastry.
reader.sourceSpanish: Llego al mostrador y pido un café americano y un pan dulce.

reader.targetFrench: Puis le serveur me donne une tasse de café au lait.
reader.supportEnglish: Then the server gives me a cup of coffee with milk.
reader.sourceSpanish: Después, el mesero me da una taza de café con leche.

reader.targetFrench: Je vérifie mon sac à emporter et je vois qu'il n'y a pas de pan dulce dedans.
reader.supportEnglish: I check my bag and see that there is no pastry in it.
reader.sourceSpanish: Reviso mi bolsa y veo que no hay pan dulce.

reader.targetFrench: D'abord, je souris et je dis : « Excusez-moi, je crois qu'il y a une erreur dans ma commande. »
reader.supportEnglish: First, I smile and say: Excuse me, I think there is a mistake with my order.
reader.sourceSpanish: Primero, sonrío y digo: Disculpe, creo que hay un error con mi pedido.

reader.targetFrench: Ensuite, j'explique : « J'ai commandé un americano, pas un café au lait. »
reader.supportEnglish: Then I explain: I ordered an americano, not a coffee with milk.
reader.sourceSpanish: Luego explico: Pedí un café americano, no un café con leche.

reader.targetFrench: Je dis aussi : « Il me manque un pan dulce, et voici mon reçu. »
reader.supportEnglish: I also say: I am missing a pastry, and here is my receipt.
reader.sourceSpanish: También digo: Me falta un pan dulce, y aquí está mi recibo.

reader.targetFrench: Je demande : « Pouvez-vous me l'échanger, s'il vous plaît ? »
reader.supportEnglish: I ask: Can you change it for me, please?
reader.sourceSpanish: Pregunto: ¿Me lo puede cambiar, por favor?

reader.targetFrench: Le serveur dit : « Bien sûr, je vous apporte le café et le pan dulce tout de suite. »
reader.supportEnglish: The server says: Of course, I will bring you the coffee and the pastry now.
reader.sourceSpanish: El mesero dice: Claro, ahora le traigo el café y el pan dulce.

forms.exampleFrench: Je commande un americano et un pan dulce.
forms.exampleEnglish: I order an americano and a pastry.
forms.explanationEnglish: French splits pedir into two verbs. Commander means to order food or drink, which is the sense used here. Demander means to ask for something (Je demande le reçu). Commander is a regular -er verb with no stem change, so the Spanish e-to-i change does not carry over. Polite form: vous commandez. Spanish usted takes third-person verb forms, but French vous is a second-person plural form with its own ending, and it is the form to use with one staff member.

forms.exampleFrench: Je vérifie mon sac à emporter et il n'y a pas de pan dulce.
forms.exampleEnglish: I check my bag and there is no pastry.
forms.explanationEnglish: Vérifier is the French verb used here for check. It is a regular -er verb; the stem vérifi- plus -ons gives nous vérifions, and the stem plus -ez gives vous vérifiez. Polite form: vous vérifiez.

forms.exampleFrench: Pouvez-vous me changer le café, s'il vous plaît ?
forms.exampleEnglish: Can you change the coffee for me, please?
forms.explanationEnglish: Changer is a regular -er verb. Nous changeons keeps the e so the g stays soft. The related verb échanger (to exchange) is used in card 14 and Reader line 7 for swapping the wrong item. Polite form: vous changez.

forms.exampleFrench: Je vous apporte le café et le pan dulce tout de suite.
forms.exampleEnglish: I will bring you the coffee and the pastry now.
forms.explanationEnglish: Apporter means to bring. It is regular, so the irregular yo form of traer (traigo) does not carry over. Before a vowel, je becomes j'. Polite form: vous apportez.

forms.exampleFrench: D'abord, je souris et je dis : « Excusez-moi. »
forms.exampleEnglish: First I smile and say: Excuse me.
forms.explanationEnglish: Dire means to say or to tell. It is irregular in French, but not in the same way as decir: there is no e-to-i change and no special je form like digo. The form to watch is vous dites, which does not end in -ez. Polite form: vous dites.

modes.promptEnglish: Write the full French sentence from memory: I am missing a pastry.

speaking.settingEnglish: You are at the counter where you just ordered an americano and a pan dulce. You already have your one receipt in hand. The server has handed you a cup of coffee with milk, and your bag has no pan dulce in it.

roles.englishDescription: You, the learner. You politely point out the mistake with your order, explain what you ordered, say what is missing, show your receipt, and ask for the coffee to be changed.
The server at the counter who hands you the wrong coffee, listens to your correction, and agrees to bring the right coffee and the missing pan dulce.

objectivesEnglish: Open politely with Excusez-moi and soften the correction with je crois que: say you think there is a mistake with your order.
Contrast the two drinks with pas: say you ordered an americano, not a café au lait.
Say what is missing with il me manque: you are missing a pan dulce.
Present the receipt you already have with Voici mon reçu.
Ask the server to change the coffee with Pouvez-vous me l'échanger, s'il vous plaît, using vous throughout.

internalNotes.note: Editorial decision, pending qualified review: pan dulce is kept in the French as a culturally named item (un pan dulce, masculine, following the Spanish) in card 6, card 13, Reader lines 1, 3, 6 and 8, the forms examples, Write mode and the speaking block. The source setting is Mexican/US Spanish and is preserved. No definitive French equivalent is claimed; viennoiserie is only a loose category word and was removed as a translation. The learner note says that in a French bakery one names the specific item. A qualified reviewer should confirm the gender choice and whether the term needs italics or a gloss in the Reader.

Editorial, pending qualified review: un americano and un café au lait are kept as source-faithful targets. Learner notes mention un café allongé and un (café) crème as common café usage in France; these are usage remarks, not asserted exact equivalents.

Source mi bolsa / my bag is the takeout bag from the counter, not the customer's own handbag. French changed from mon sac to mon sac à emporter so the scene stays logical; dedans added in Reader line 3 to match 'in it'. Editorial alternative for the reviewer: le sachet. English and Spanish support lines are unchanged from the source.

Register aligned to the source: puede is plain present, so Pourriez-vous was changed to Pouvez-vous, matching card 16. Échanger is used for swapping the item while the forms table teaches changer for cambiar; this pairing is editorial and pending qualified review (alternative: Pouvez-vous me le changer).

A vous row was added to all five verbs because every customer line uses vous; Spanish usted (third person) maps to French vous (second-person plural form). Pedir is split between commander (order food or drink, used here) and demander (ask for). The vérifier explanation was corrected: it is a regular -er verb, not a separate -ier class. Form IDs core:10:form:<source verb> were added; they are new, not from the source.

Six authored modes, each targetFrench identical to its source card. Mode IDs core:10:mode:1 to core:10:mode:6 were added. Prompts for Recall and Type now ask for the article the answer contains. Type is a single term; Write is a full sentence (moved from card 6 to card 13) so the two modes differ. This distinction is editorial and pending review.

The speaking block was rebuilt around the pinned passage: counter setting, wrong coffee, missing pan dulce, one receipt already in hand. The earlier family-ordering scenario (wife, son, mother-in-law, sans, asking for the check) was unrelated to this lesson and was removed, along with its reference to an unpinned speaking specification. Reader narration stays first-person je.

Corrections against the old draft: line 4 now opens D'abord, to match the forms example; line 5 uses Ensuite for Luego so it no longer repeats Puis from line 2; line 6 uses Je dis aussi for También digo instead of J'ajoute. Earlier drift fixes are retained: Il me manque, Je vérifie, and dit in line 8.

French spacing is encoded explicitly: U+00A0 before colons, U+202F before question marks and semicolons and inside guillemets. Answer matching for Type, Write and Say should normalise these to ordinary spaces before comparison. Encoding to be confirmed before any registration.
